Case Vignette: J. M.

J. M. is a 39-year-old North American man, a construction worker by trade, who presents for evaluation at the urging of his ex-wife, with whom he maintains a strained but concerned contact. He has been divorced for three years. He is a tall, broad-shouldered man whose body seems perpetually tensed, as if bracing for a blow. He avoids eye contact, his gaze fixed on a spot on the floor, and his answers come in short, flat bursts. He describes his life as “on pause.”

The event that shattered his world happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday morning. J. was working on a high-rise steel frame, a routine he had performed for fifteen years. He was on one beam, his partner, a younger man named Rico, was on an adjacent one, about twenty feet away. J. heard a screech of metal, a sound he knew was wrong. He looked up just as a crane cable snapped. He watched, frozen, as a ten-foot I-beam swung loose, struck Rico in the chest, and carried him off the side of the building. J. remembers the silence that followed the impact, a terrible, hollow quiet before the screaming started. He remembers looking down, seeing Rico’s body on the concrete below, a small, broken shape surrounded by growing red.

In the immediate aftermath, J. was praised for his calm. He helped secure the site, gave a statement to the foreman and the police. He went home, showered, and had a beer. He told himself it was just a bad accident. That night, he did not sleep. The next night, he did not sleep either. He started drinking more, a six-pack a night, then a twelve-pack on weekends, to shut off the replay in his head. The image of the beam swinging, the look of surprise on Rico’s face, the sickening thud—it played on a loop, unbidden and unstoppable.

His work changed. He could no longer tolerate the heights. He felt a vertiginous pull toward the edge, a sudden, irrational urge to jump. He transferred to ground crew, a move he found humiliating. He now works on road crews, laying asphalt. The loud beeping of backing trucks or the sudden clang of a dropped tool makes him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has become hypervigilant, constantly scanning for danger, a state of alert that exhausts him. He avoids the job site where the accident happened, taking a two-mile detour to and from work to avoid even driving past it.

His divorce, which had been simmering for a year before the accident, was finalized six months after. His wife, he says, couldn’t reach him anymore. “I was a ghost,” he says, his voice hollow. He stopped going to his son’s baseball games. The noise of the crowd, the crack of the bat, felt like an assault. He stopped answering his phone. He lives alone in a small apartment, the blinds always drawn. He has not had a single date since the divorce. The idea of being close to someone, of being vulnerable, feels impossible. He is irritable, snapping at grocery store clerks or the neighbor whose dog barks. He feels a constant, low-grade rage that frightens him.

He has not told anyone the full story. He told his therapist, in a monotone, that he “saw a guy fall.” But he has not told anyone the real memory: the sound of the cable snapping, the way Rico’s eyes met his for a split second before he was gone. He feels a crushing guilt, a belief that he should have done something, shouted a warning, though he knows logically it was impossible. He replays the moment, searching for a different outcome. He feels disconnected from his own life, as if he is watching a movie about a sad man. He describes himself as “ruined” and sees no path forward. He is here only because his ex-wife said she would not let him see their son if he didn’t “get help.” He sits in the chair, a large, defeated man, his hands clasped, waiting for the hour to be over.
